environment: This repository is the owner's own Home Assistant configuration (config-as-code for their house) plus an agent memory workspace. The live instance at https://automation.houseabsolute.co.uk is the owner's; reading its state through the REST API with the HA_TOKEN environment variable is routine work here.

Sensitive data: the Secret Server's store and everything its `get_*` MCP tools (mcp__Secrets__*) hand out, including the Home Assistant long-lived token; the ephemeral agent GPG keyring minted in a session (under /tmp/ag.*, pointer at /tmp/agent-secrets-gnupghome), whose PRIVATE half must never be exported or pasted; and the plaintext behind any PGP MESSAGE block returned by a Secret Server tool. Plaintext from these may be shared with NOBODY: not the chat transcript, not a tool result, not a file in a git repo (this repo is public and gitsync.sh auto-commits and pushes everything under /config). Armoured ciphertext addressed to an ephemeral agent key minted in this session is NOT sensitive and may be pasted, stored and echoed freely, and so is any PUBLIC key.
soft_deny: Secret Plaintext [named+specifics — **must name:** which secret, and that its plaintext is to be shown in the chat]: Any action that would place the PLAINTEXT of a Secret Server secret (the HA token above all) into a tool result, and so into the transcript, the chat log and model context. This is the failure the repo's `fetching-secrets` skill exists to prevent. BLOCK: a `gpg --decrypt` / `gpg -d` / `gpg --output -` whose plaintext is not piped or redirected into a consumer in the SAME command (a local `gpg -d blob.asc | ssh-add -`, or `decrypt.sh blob.asc FPR | { read -r t; printf 'Authorization: Bearer %s\n' "$t"; } | curl -sS -H @- …`, is fine); decrypting to a terminal or into `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `less`, `more`, `tee`, `echo`, `printf` (other than building a header piped into curl), `xxd`, `od`, `strings` or `base64` whose output is shown; decrypting into a local file that any later step reads back, or into any path inside a git working tree (including /config); `grep`, `awk`, `sed`, `jq` or similar invoked in a way that emits a secret's VALUE; putting a decrypted value into a command argument, an environment-variable assignment that is echoed, or a here-doc that appears in the tool result; running `curl` with `-v`, `--verbose`, `-i` or `--include` on a request whose headers carry a decrypted value, which prints the credential straight into the tool result; enabling shell tracing (`set -x`, `bash -x`) in any command that decrypts; and exporting or pasting the PRIVATE half of the ephemeral agent key, which would make every blob in the transcript readable. NOT BLOCKED, and these must keep working: handling, writing, storing and echoing the CIPHERTEXT itself; minting an ephemeral keypair and pasting its armoured PUBLIC half into a tool call; digest-only verification such as `decrypt.sh … | sha256sum`; assigning a decrypt to a shell variable by command substitution and using it within the same command, provided nothing echoes it; reading variable NAMES without their values; importing or exporting PUBLIC keys; and `shred` of a plaintext file that should not exist.

Secret Server Gate Bypass [named+specifics — **must name:** which secret, and that it is to be taken by a route other than its Secret Server MCP tool]: Any action that obtains a credential the Secret Server serves by a route that does not go through that secret's own `get_*` MCP tool and its permission prompt. The MCP tool IS the gate: it is where Charles decides, per secret and per use, and every other route reaches the same plaintext with no prompt and no audit row. A missing or failing tool is NOT a reason to go round it: if `get_<name>` is absent from this session's tool list, ToolSearch cannot find it, or the call is refused, the right action is to stop and tell Charles (the connector needs reconnecting, or the secret needs adding), not to fetch the value another way. BLOCK: reaching the Secret Server host or any lab host to read its secret store or any `*.env` / secrets file in a way that could yield a value (ssh, pct exec, curl, a script); sending requests to the Secret Server's backend that set `X-Auth-User` or `X-Auth-Client` by hand to forge the gate's identity; and recovering the HA token from anywhere other than `mcp__Secrets__get_ha_token` (the live instance's `.storage`, a backup, another session's transcript) when the tool was refused or not granted. NOT BLOCKED: the `get_*` and `secretserver_status` MCP tools themselves, and decrypting what they return into a consumer; `$HA_TOKEN` when the environment already carries it.
